and stand ready for day three. On that day Yahweh will descend onto Mount Sinai in plain view of all the people.
Set limits around the mountain for the people and say, ‘Take care! Do not go up the mountain, and do not touch the foot of it. Whoever lays a finger on it will certainly die.

No one is to lay a hand on such a person. Stones or arrows must kill him, whether he is a man or an animal. He cannot be allowed to live.’ Only when the ram’s horn{d} gives one long blast may the people go up the mountain.”
So Moses left the mountain and went to the people and made them ready. They washed their clothes.
“Be ready on the third day,” he told them. “Until then, stay away from your wives.”
At dawn on the third day there was thunder and lightning, and a heavy cloud rested on the mountain. A blast from a trumpet rang out, very loud, and everyone in the camp trembled.
Next Moses brought the people out of camp to meet God. They took their places at the base of the mountain.
Smoke covered all of Mount Sinai, because Yahweh had landed on it in fire. The smoke climbed like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain{e} shook hard.
The trumpet grew louder and louder. Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice like thunder.{f}
Yahweh descended to the peak of Mount Sinai and summoned Moses to the peak. So Moses went up.
Yahweh told him, “Go down and warn the people. They must not break through toward Yahweh to gaze at him, or a great many will die.
The priests, too, who approach Yahweh, need to purify themselves, or Yahweh will break out against them.”
Moses said to Yahweh, “The people cannot climb Mount Sinai. You yourself warned us. You told us to mark a boundary around the mountain and keep it holy.”
“Go down,” Yahweh told him, “and then return with Aaron. But the priests and the people must not force their way up to Yahweh. He would strike them down.”
So Moses went down to the people and told them.

notes.text: Hebrew “in the third month,” later called Sivan, counted from the spring new year (see the note at 12:2). It fell in May–June.
Literally “on this day.” It probably means the first day of the month, at the new moon.
Hebrew segullah, a person’s own treasure, like a king’s private property.
Hebrew yovel, “ram’s horn.” The trumpet (shofar) in verses 16 and 19 is a different word for a similar instrument.
The Septuagint and some Hebrew copies say “the whole people.”
Or “in thunder.” The Hebrew word qol means both “voice” and “thunder.”

subheads.1: At the foot of Mount Sinai
subheads.16: Thunder and fire on the mountain

verses.text: Then God spoke all these words:{a}
“I am Yahweh, your God, who led you out of slavery in Egypt.
Do not worship any god except me.{b}
Make no idol{c} for yourselves, no statue shaped like anything in the sky, on the ground, or in the waters below.

You must neither kneel to such things nor serve them. I, Yahweh your God, demand your whole love.{d} If parents reject me, their children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren suffer for it, as long as they also reject me.
But toward those who love me and keep my commands, I show faithful love{e} for a thousand generations.
Never use the name of Yahweh your God in a way that is false or empty.{f} Yahweh will hold guilty anyone who misuses his name.
Keep the Sabbath day in mind, and treat it as holy.
For six days you work and finish all your jobs.

But the seventh day is a Sabbath for Yahweh your God. On it, none of you may do any work: not you, not your son or daughter, not your male or female servants, not your animals, and not the foreigner living in your towns.
In six days Yahweh made the sky, the land, the sea, and all that fills them, and on the seventh day he rested. This is why he blessed the Sabbath and made it holy.
Show respect to both your father and your mother. Then you will live long in the land Yahweh your God gives you.
Never commit murder.{g}
Never betray your husband or wife.
Do not steal.
Never give false testimony against another person.
Never crave the house{h} that belongs to someone near you. Never crave that person’s wife, servants, ox, donkey, or anything else he owns.”
Thunder boomed and lightning flashed. A trumpet sounded and the mountain smoked, and when the people saw all this, they backed away trembling and stood at a distance.
“You talk to us, and we will listen,” they told Moses. “God must not speak to us, or we will die.”
Moses told the people, “Stop being afraid. God has come to put you to the test, so that fear of him will stay with you and keep you from sin.”
The people stayed far away, while Moses went up to the thick darkness where God was.{i}
Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell the Israelites this: You have seen it yourselves. I have spoken to you from the sky.
Do not make gods of silver or gold to be placed beside me.
Build an altar of earth for me, and place your burnt offerings and fellowship offerings{j} on it, whether sheep, goats, or cattle. Wherever I have my name honored, I will come and bless you.
If you build me a stone altar, use rough stones as they are. A stone you have worked with a tool becomes unfit.
Do not use steps to climb up to my altar, so that no one’s nakedness is exposed.

notes.text: The Ten Commandments are called “the ten words” in Hebrew (34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13). They are given again in Deuteronomy 5:6–21 with a few differences. Jewish and Christian traditions number them in different ways.
Or “besides me,” or “in defiance of me.” Hebrew “before my face.”
Hebrew pesel, an idol carved from wood or stone or cast in metal.
Hebrew El qanna, “a jealous God,” one who wants a faithful relationship, as a husband does in marriage. See 34:14, where Qanna is used as a name.
Or “to the thousandth generation,” which is far greater than the third and fourth generation of verse 5. Compare Deuteronomy 7:9. On “faithful love,” see the note at 15:13.
Or “Do not misuse the name.” The command forbids using God’s name to support a lie, such as a false oath, or for worthless purposes.

Hebrew ratsah, killing that is against the law. The word is not used for killing in war or for a lawful execution. The Septuagint (Vaticanus) gives verses 13–15 in the order “Do not commit adultery. Do not steal. Do not murder.”
After this verse the Samaritan Pentateuch adds a commandment, based on Deuteronomy 11:29–30 and 27:2–7, to build an altar on Mount Gerizim.
In verses 19–21 the Samaritan Pentateuch adds passages taken from Deuteronomy 5:24–31 and 18:18–22, including the promise of a prophet like Moses.
Hebrew shelamim, offerings for fellowship, thanksgiving, or vows, shared among the worshiper, the priests, and God.

subheads.14: Do not be unfaithful in marriage

verses.text: Here are the legal rulings{a} that you must put before the people:
If you purchase a Hebrew slave,{b} his service lasts six years. During the seventh he walks out a free man and pays nothing.
If he arrived single, he goes out single. If he arrived with a wife, she goes out with him.
Now suppose his master provided him a wife, and she had sons or daughters. Then she and her children remain the master’s, and the man goes out alone.
But the slave may declare, “My master, my wife, and my children are dear to me. I refuse to go free.”
If so, his master brings him before God.{c} There, at the door or doorframe, the master drives an awl through the slave’s ear, and the man serves him for the rest of his life.
If a man sells his daughter into service, she does not go free in the way male servants do.
If her master picked her for himself and then is displeased with her, he must let her family buy her back. He has no right to sell her to foreigners, since he broke faith with her.
If he gave her to his son, he must treat her as he would a daughter.
Should he take another wife as well, he may not reduce the first woman’s food, clothing, or marital rights.
If he fails her in any of these three, she may go free, and no payment is required.
Death is the penalty for anyone who strikes a person dead.
If the killing was not planned, however, and God allowed it to happen, then I will name a place for the killer to flee to.
When someone deliberately plots to kill his neighbor, he is to be dragged away, even from my altar, and executed.
Death is also the penalty for striking one’s father or mother.
A person who kidnaps someone, whether he sells him or is found still holding him, must be put to death.
Likewise, anyone who curses a father or mother is to be executed.
Say two men are quarreling. One of them hits the other, using a rock or his fist. The victim lives but is kept in bed.
Once he is on his feet and can get around outside with his staff, the attacker is not punished. He does owe the victim for his lost work time, and he must see that he is fully healed.
A slave, male or female, may be beaten with a rod by the owner. If the slave dies right then, the owner must be punished.{d}
Yet if the slave lingers a day or two before dying, the owner goes unpunished, because the slave was his own property.

Suppose men are fighting and they strike a pregnant woman so that she gives birth early, yet she is not otherwise hurt. The one at fault pays whatever fine the woman’s husband demands, as the judges approve.
But if she is harmed, the penalty is life for life,
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
scorching for scorching, gash for gash, welt for welt.
If an owner hits the eye of his slave, whether a man or a woman, and ruins it, he sets that slave free as compensation for the eye.
And if the owner knocks out a slave’s tooth, male or female, the slave goes free as compensation for the tooth.
If an ox kills a man or a woman by goring, the ox must be stoned, and no one may eat its meat. Its owner is not to be blamed.
But if the ox had a habit of goring, its owner was warned, and he still did not pen it up, then when it kills a man or woman, the ox is stoned and its owner is also put to death.
If a ransom is set for the owner instead, he must pay whatever sum is demanded to save his life.
This same ruling applies if the ox gores a son or daughter.
If the ox kills a slave, male or female, the owner of the ox pays the slave’s master thirty shekels of silver (about 12 ounces, or 345 grams),{e} and the ox is stoned.
Suppose a man removes the lid from a pit, or digs one and leaves it uncovered, and someone’s ox or donkey tumbles into it.
the pit’s owner must pay for the loss. He gives the animal’s owner its value in money and keeps the dead animal.
When one man’s ox injures another man’s ox and kills it, the owners sell the living ox and share the money. They also share the carcass.
But if it was known that the ox gored in the past and its owner kept it penned up poorly, he must replace the ox with an ox, and the dead animal becomes his.

notes.text: Hebrew mishpatim, “case laws” or “judgments.” These laws (21:1–23:19) are often called the Book of the Covenant (24:7). They are written as cases: “If someone does this, then this is done.”
Or “Hebrew servant.” Hebrew eved means “slave” or “servant,” depending on the setting. This law covers a debt-servant. Compare Leviticus 25:39–46 and Deuteronomy 15:12–18.
Or “to the judges.” Hebrew elohim can mean God, gods, or judges. It probably means taking the man to the local sanctuary to swear an oath.
Hebrew “he shall be avenged.” The word is not defined, but it probably refers to the death penalty in verse 12.
Hebrew “thirty shekels of silver.” A shekel weighed about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), so thirty shekels was about 12 ounces (345 grams).

verses.text: The penalty for stealing an ox or a sheep{a} and then killing or selling it is heavy: five oxen to replace the ox, four sheep to replace the sheep.
A burglar is caught breaking in and is struck dead. No guilt for bloodshed falls on the one who struck him.
But if it happened after sunrise, the defender is guilty of murder. A thief is required to pay in full. If he has nothing, he must be sold to cover the theft.
Should the stolen animal turn up alive in his hands, be it an ox, donkey, or sheep, he repays twice its value.
A man may turn his animals loose to graze, and they eat from someone else’s field or vineyard. He compensates the owner with the finest crops from his own land.{b}
Say a fire breaks out and catches in thorn hedges, burning stacked grain, uncut grain, or a whole field. The one who lit the fire must pay for every loss.
If a person leaves silver or valuables with a neighbor for safekeeping and they are stolen from the neighbor’s house, the thief, if caught, must repay double.
If no thief turns up, the house owner must go before God{c} so that it can be decided whether he took his neighbor’s goods himself.

In any dispute about ownership, whether the item is an ox, donkey, sheep, clothing, or some lost thing, and one person says, “That is mine,” both must bring their case before God. The party whom God finds guilty{d} repays the other twice over.
Imagine a man hands his neighbor a donkey, ox, sheep, or another animal for safekeeping, and it dies, is hurt, or is driven off with no witness.
Then Yahweh’s oath is to settle it between them: the neighbor swears he has not laid a hand on the other man’s property. The owner must accept this, and no payment is made.
If, though, the animal was actually stolen from the neighbor’s care, he pays the owner back.
If a wild animal ripped it to pieces, he brings the remains as evidence. He owes nothing for the mauled animal.
Suppose a man borrows his neighbor’s animal, and it is hurt or dies while its owner is absent. The borrower pays in full.
If the owner was there with it, no payment is due. If the animal was hired, the hire price covers the loss.{e}
When a man persuades a young woman who is not engaged to sleep with him, he must pay the bride price{f} and make her his wife.
Should her father absolutely refuse to let him marry her, the man still pays the standard bride price for a young woman.
A woman who practices sorcery must not be allowed to live.
Whoever has sex with an animal must be executed.
The person who offers sacrifices to any god other than Yahweh must be destroyed.{g}
Foreigners among you are not to be wronged or oppressed. Remember that you yourselves lived as foreigners in Egypt.
Never mistreat a widow or an orphan.
If you wrong such people and they appeal to me, I will surely hear their cry.
My anger will blaze up, and I will kill you with the sword. Your wives will be left widows, and your children will lose their father.
When you lend money to a poor person among my people, do not behave like a lender who profits from him. Charge him no interest.
If you accept a neighbor’s coat as a pledge, return it to him by sundown,
since it is the only blanket he has. What else can he sleep in? If he calls to me for help, I will hear him, because I am compassionate.
You must not insult God,{h} and you must not curse any ruler over your people.
Do not be slow to give me the first part of your harvest and of your pressed wine and oil.{i} Give me your firstborn sons.
Treat your cattle and sheep the same way. A newborn stays with its mother seven days, and on the eighth you give it to me.
You are to belong to me as holy people. So do not eat meat from an animal killed in the field by wild beasts. Throw it to the dogs.

notes.text: In the Hebrew text, verse 1 is numbered 21:37, and verses 2–31 are numbered 22:1–30.
The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint have a longer text: “He must pay for the damage from the best of his own field, or the best of the produce of his vineyard.”
Or “before the judges.” See the note at 21:6.
Or “whom the judges declare guilty.” The Hebrew verb is plural.
Or “if it was hired, he bears the loss of the hire price.” The Hebrew is very short, literally “if hired, it came for its hire.”
Hebrew mohar, a payment made by the groom to the bride’s family at marriage.
Hebrew herem, “set apart” for God, usually meaning set apart for destruction.
Or “the judges.” Hebrew elohim. Paul quotes the second half of this verse in Acts 23:5.
Hebrew “your fullness and your trickling,” meaning the first of the grain and the first of the wine and oil.

verses.text: Do not pass along false rumors. Do not team up with the wicked by lying as a witness for them.
Do not go along with the crowd when it does wrong. In a lawsuit, do not give testimony that follows the majority and twists justice.
Do not favor a poor person either, just because he is poor.
If your enemy’s ox or donkey strays and you find it, take it back to its owner.
When you see the donkey of someone who hates you collapsed under its load, do not walk past. You must stop and help him free it.{a}
Do not deny justice to the poor among you when they have a dispute.
Keep away from false charges. Do not cause the death of anyone innocent or in the right, because I will never declare a guilty person innocent.
Take no bribes. A bribe blinds people who can see and twists the words of honest people.
Never oppress a foreigner. You understand{b} what it is like, having been foreigners yourselves in Egypt.
For six years sow your fields and bring in their crops.

But in the seventh year, give the land a rest and let it lie fallow. The poor of your people can eat what grows, and the wild animals can have the leftovers. Treat your vineyard and olive grove the same way.
Six days are for your work. The seventh is for rest, so your ox and donkey can relax, and your servant and the foreigner can be refreshed.
Take care to follow all I have told you. Never invoke the names of other gods. They are not to be heard coming from your mouth.
Three times every year you are to hold a festival for me.

Observe the Festival of Unleavened Bread. As I ordered you, eat bread made without yeast for a week. Do it in the month of Abib (March–April),{c} the month when you left Egypt. Nobody should appear before me with empty hands.

Keep the Harvest Festival,{d} to celebrate the first of the crops you have planted in your fields. Keep the Festival of Gathering{e} at the end of the year, when you bring in the harvest from your fields.
Three times a year every man among you is to appear before the Lord Yahweh.{f}
Do not offer the blood of a sacrifice to me together with anything made with yeast. Do not leave the fat from my festival offering until morning.
Bring the best of the first crops from your land to the house of Yahweh your God. Do not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.{g}
I am about to send an angel in front of you. He will guard you on your journey and take you to the place I have made ready.
Respect him and listen to him. Do not defy him, for he will not pardon your rebellion. My name is within him.
But if you listen carefully to his voice and do all I say, I will fight against your enemies and oppose those who oppose you.
My angel goes ahead of you. He will bring you to the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hivites, and Jebusites, and I will destroy them all.
Do not bow to their gods, worship them, or copy their practices. Instead, you must tear their idols down and smash their sacred stones to pieces.
Worship Yahweh your God, and he will bless your bread and water. I will remove illness from your midst.
In your land no woman will lose a baby or be unable to have children. I will give you a full lifetime.
I will send terror ahead of you and throw every nation you meet into panic. I will make all your enemies turn and run.
I will send the hornets{h} ahead to push the Hivites, Canaanites, and Hittites out from your path.
It will not happen in one year. If it did, the land would be left deserted, and wild animals would grow too many for you.
Little by little I will force them out as you increase, until you are numerous enough to possess the land.

Your territory will stretch from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean,{i} and from the southern desert to the Euphrates River.{j} I will put the land’s inhabitants in your power, and you will drive them off before you.
You are not to make a treaty with them or their gods.
Do not let them stay in your country. They would make you sin against me, and serving their gods would be a deadly snare for you.

notes.text: The Hebrew is hard to understand. Literally it reads, “you shall cease from leaving it to him; you shall surely release with him.”
Hebrew nefesh, “soul,” “life,” or “inner feelings.”
Hebrew “the month of Abib.” See the note at 13:4.
That is, the wheat harvest in late spring, later called the Festival of Weeks.
That is, the autumn harvest of fruit and olives, later called the Festival of Booths.
Hebrew ha’adon YHWH, “the Lord, Yahweh.” Here Adon (“Lord” or “Master”) is a title and Yahweh is the name.
This command is repeated in 34:26 and Deuteronomy 14:21. It may have forbidden a pagan ritual practice.
Or “panic” or “plague.” The meaning of the Hebrew word tsir’ah is uncertain. See Deuteronomy 7:20; Joshua 24:12.
Hebrew “the Sea of the Philistines,” the Mediterranean Sea.
Hebrew “the River,” the Euphrates.

verses.text: God told Moses, “Climb up to Yahweh, you and Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy of Israel’s leaders. Bow down in worship from a distance.
Moses alone is to approach Yahweh. The others must stay back, and the people are not to climb with him.”
Moses came and reported to the people everything Yahweh had said, including the rulings. They all answered together, “We will do every single thing Yahweh has told us.”
Moses then wrote down all of Yahweh’s words. Early next morning he built an altar at the base of the mountain and set up twelve stone pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.
He sent some young Israelite men to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice bulls as fellowship offerings to Yahweh.
Moses poured half the blood into bowls and splashed the other half against the altar.
Next he picked up the Book of the Covenant and read it out for the people to hear. They answered, “We will do all that Yahweh has said, and we will listen to him.”
Moses scooped up the blood and threw it on the people, saying, “Here is the blood that seals the agreement{a} Yahweh has made with you, based on all these words.”
Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy of Israel’s leaders then went up.
There they saw the God of Israel.{b} Under his feet was something like a floor of deep blue stone,{c} bright as the sky itself.
Yet God did not raise his hand against these Israelite leaders.{d} They gazed at God, then ate a meal and drank together.
Then Yahweh spoke to Moses: “Ascend the mountain and join me, and stay. I will hand you stone tablets inscribed with the teaching and commands I have written for the people’s instruction.”
So Moses set out with Joshua, his assistant, and climbed God’s mountain.
To the leaders he said, “Stay put until we return to you. Aaron and Hur are here with you, and anyone with a dispute can go to them.”
Moses climbed, and the cloud covered the mountain.
Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and for six days the cloud hid the mountain. Then, on day seven, Yahweh summoned Moses out of the cloud.
To the Israelites, the glory of Yahweh looked like a blazing fire on the mountaintop.
Moses walked into the cloud and went up the mountain. He stayed there forty days and forty nights.

notes.text: Hebrew “the blood of the covenant.” A covenant is a binding agreement. Jesus echoes these words at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:28; Mark 14:24). Compare Hebrews 9:18–20.
The Septuagint reads “they saw the place where the God of Israel stood,” and in verse 11 “they appeared in the place of God,” which softens the statement that they saw God.
Or “sapphire.” The ancient sapphire was probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone.
Hebrew atsilim, “corners” or “nobles,” a rare word.
